utterances.text: They let us use Qafa Pruset. It's much closer to where we live. That would be much closer from Gjakova but in order to make the journey harder for us, they took us all around, that way and over that crossing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, without disturbing what's on the ELMO, just leave it there, could the court deputy bring up on the e-court system, P23? Now, Mr. Lukic, I doubt if you're going to advance this matter further with this witness because there you see a map with the same point given the name that the witness has given it. It may be a matter for further investigation, I quite accept, but do you think that there is anything further to be learned from the matter with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously it would be very hard although we have a map that has completely different markings than this one shown on the screen. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, are you aware of the fact that on the 9th of April, on the front line from the village Deve to Kushar, an infantry attack was launched from Albania and that for that reason, units of the Yugoslav army moved into the sector of your village, which is actually near the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about that at all. It's the first time I hear about it too. Our village was surrounded. I don't know whether they were around our house for three or four hours but about that. My house is near to the town, to Gjakova, not close to the border really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic are you going to indicate a date on which the army moved into the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour, April the 9th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The day when the attack started and the enforcement came in. That's the information we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But anyways, the witness said she's not aware of it so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stated that NATO never targeted the area around your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO never bombarded, never bombed our village or around the village except kasanas [phoen] where the army was deployed. But not our village. It never attacked the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This Defence is in possession of some information that NATO in that very area used cluster bombs with depleted uranium. This is official data which is easy to prove. Do you change your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think he's entitled to indicate the basis on which he poses the question. Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put such data before you, would that affect your testimony? Would you change anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have a date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to assist, Mr. Lukic? It's not obligatory because the question -- the answer the witness gave was "never" and therefore the date is not material, but if you have a date then obviously it does assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have a date but I have a time frame, from the beginning of the bombing until the end, it was bombed, that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just thought it would make a difference if it were before the 27th of April or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 24th of March is before the 27th April. I said from the beginning of the bombardment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Your data, to be of significance, would have to predate the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, did you know that between the 24th of March 1999 and the 27th of April, 1999, NATO bombed the area in which your village is?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't happen in our area that NATO bombed, not even the neighbouring village, Guske. No, Nec. What is around our village? None of these villages was bombed. Up until the 27th, when I was there, it didn't happen. After the 27th, it may have happened because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Malaj. I would kindly ask the Registry to show us the fourth page of 6D13 on the screen, the fourth page of 6D13. In the meantime I wanted to ask you this: Do you know the person by the name of Krasnici [phoen], Lus?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: L-u-s-h.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know him. If you want me to tell you about him, he's a member of the association, The 27th of April, because he has been dealing with the corpses of the families who lost their loved ones in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This NGO, did it submit some sort of an indictment to this Tribunal against the alleged perpetrators of these murders?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe. I don't know what they have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to number 34 on the list, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this your name at number 34 of the list?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you contacted by the people of that organisation concerning your testimony in a potential case they tried to set up for --

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: For testimony, for statements, but for issues concerning the missing. The names that I'm looking at on the screen, they are members who were missing up until 2004 and after that their corpses, one by one, have been returned to us, and five members of my family have so far been returned: My husband, my son, my nephew, and so on. I don't know what to say. This is why we appear on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say that on the list you are looking at, there are names of those missing?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names on the list, our children are missing, Maria Malaj, for example, it's my husband and my son were killed. Maria Malaj has also members of her family but there are other members, relatives, in my family. In our Malaj family there are seven who were killed but we've only received five corpses that we have buried. And there are also members of the Kabashi family. And that's why the heads of the respective families appear on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 35, Maria Malaj, this is a missing person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. She is saying these are the heads of families whose relatives are missing. Let's get on with this and not make it more distressing than it needs to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Page 49, line 3, [In English] List our children are missing. That's why I was confused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But there has been -- I understand that but it's been clarified since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell me who is Maria Malaj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic just read the transcript a little earlier and it tells you who she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It says Maria Malaj, also members of her family, that there are other members, relatives. In our family there were seven who were killed. That's why the heads of the respective families appear on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whether the people from this organisation got in touch with you, did you consent to testify?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the compiling of this list?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who carried out the investigation which resulted in this list, in the drafting of this list?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigations, I don't know. I haven't taken part in them. In this list, you can find names of the heads of families who have suffered losses. Klaudia the daughter of Maria Malaj, she was killed and she was killed as she was walking, behind her back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a general question to conclude with. You had the opportunity to go to Djakovica. I presume you're familiar with the town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: When are you saying that I went to Gjakova in during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, I didn't -- I didn't go to Gjakova, and I didn't dare to do that because there were many check-points on the way. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Djakovica after the war?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, yes, I was free. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Kodra e Cabratit is?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I've suffered a lot of wounds there. My son was injured by a mine which you had planted, and that's how I heard of -- and heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that a part of Djakovica town? Cabrat?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is a part just above the old town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which? Cabrat?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Cabrat is as you enter the city on the left-hand side. The old Carsija is on the right-hand side. Now I've learned a lot about the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But nevertheless, that is one of the neighbourhoods of the town, this Cabrat?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Malaj, for having dedicated your time to testify, and I would like to apologise if any of my questions were difficult for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mrs. Malaj, the reference to your son being injured by a mine, is that a different son from the one who has disappeared or who was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one who disappeared, he couldn't be there because he disappeared, but it's the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that but we have no date. I just wonder if it's something that happened to him before he was killed, but it's not. It's something that happened to your other son. Thank you. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second son. He was 11, Bekim Malaj, his name is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj I just want to ask you on when you left on the 27th of April and the 28th of April, you went to Prizren, correct?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you went to Kukes in Albania?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I see from looking on the map and from what you said in your statement, you took the main road from Prizren to Kukes, correct?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the main road, the one we followed. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Whatever the name of the border crossing is between Prizren and Kukes, whether it's Vrbnica or Qafa e Morines is that the place where you crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, before you continue with your questions, only one administrative thing. I don't know actually, do I have to propose the documents we tendered because, according to the court deputy, we were advised to propose those documents to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which document are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Marked map which is P35, marked by the witness. And this 6D 13, the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be done, Mr. Lukic, in relation to the marked map which is P35, and it will be given an IC number related to P35 to indicate it's a marked copy of that map. For the avoidance of any difficulty in the future it would be helpful where a marked document is tendered, in other words a document which already is in the system, but is marked by a witness, is being tendered as an exhibit in itself, if it's done at the time when it's being used rather than at the end of the evidence. As far as the other document is concerned, it's already in the system, it's been used in the case, it's not been objected to and therefore it's an exhibit according to the rules we've been following so far. Judge Nosworthy has some questions for you. Judge Nosworthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very kindly. Mrs. Malaj, I'd like to ask you about the NATO bombing. Now, you indicated in your evidence earlier on that you had not seen bombs but you had heard a bomb. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I do not know where the bombs fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: That is what I had wanted to ask you, if you were able to say how far away the bomb that you heard was. You're not able to say?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And based on what you heard, the bombing that you heard, did you do anything at all as a result of that, what you heard, in terms of your family or yourself?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Done anything, you mean? Us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What I want to know, were you affected in any way by the bomb that you heard and did you take any precaution or do anything as a result of what you heard?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was needed for our safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a good thing for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe because we started feeling safer when NATO intervened but then soon after the NATO intervention, the Serb forces were used, taking advantage of the situation against us the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Malaj, Judge Chowhan also has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you must be very tired but the question is that you gave us an impression here that KLA was not active in your village but the way it is put is as if you are completely oblivious of what KLA was. My question is do you -- do you know what KLA was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't know then, and I wanted very much to see who they were. I very much wanted to see who they were but I didn't know anything about them at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: At that time. I mean, it is being said that -- whether rightly or wrongly this is to be seen -- that KLA was active elsewhere, perhaps, if not in your village but you didn't even hear a gossip about KLA, what this organisation was, and what it was pitted against, and whether anybody from your area had interest in it or not or it was completely lack of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know anything, as I said earlier, because I was confined to the narrow circle of my family and had had no opportunity to see them or to hear about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much but you said that the men folks went to the mountains because the ambience or the atmosphere there was very tense. Why was it then tense? I mean, were people fighting or were there only directions being issued on that account? What do you -- could you explain why the atmosphere was very tense there and what were the forces who were making it tense?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The orders came from Dragan, but our men were not armed, they -- they were like civilians, like I'm here today dressed. They were dressed as civilians and they left home because they were ordered to leave home. And they left and they came back and they left and they came back. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And there was no talk about it, why this was happening?

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, when men left at night, we could hear gunshots, and the -- our men were left -- left because whenever they wanted to do something, the Serbian forces started an operation at 3, 4, in the morning, and they completed it by dawn, and it was during that period that men tried to avoid, and that was on the orders of Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I should thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lizane Malaj [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Malaj, that brings your evidence to an end. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for the understanding and everything else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sabbah, could we very briefly go into private session? The reason -- just hold on a second. The reason for that relates to the personal circumstances of the next witness and also in relation to one matter I wish to raise with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Deda, would you please stand and would you repeat the words set out on the card in front of you, the words of the solemn declaration? On you go. Just read it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Now, we know that you have provided information as requested in the past, but as is the case with all the witnesses who will give evidence in this case, as presently advised, it's still necessary for you to come here to be asked questions, and that's the exercise which will be conducted today. Some of these questions you may find challenge what you are saying, and if that happens, please bear in mind that the counsel, the lawyers who are asking these questions, are doing a job as professional persons. It is their job to ask difficult questions and awkward questions, depending on the circumstances. It's a system you may not be familiar with but it's the system which operates in this Tribunal. And it's as well you know before we start that sometimes the questions may be difficult and you may find that they to some extent challenge what you've said but bear in mind that that happens with every witness and bear in mind also that if we consider any conduct by anyone in the Court is not proper, then we as judges will intervene to deal with that situation. Now the first person who will ask you questions is Mr. Hannis, the Prosecutor. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you tell us your name, please, for the record?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Merita Deda.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Ms. Deda, I understand from your statement that in early 1999, you lived in the village of Guske in Gjakova municipality in Kosovo with your family. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was -- who were the members of your family who lived with you there at that time?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: My father, my mother, two sisters, two brothers, an uncle and his wife, and their three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to have the witness shown her 92 bis package which is Exhibit P2233 and again I have a hard copy that we can show her.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Deda if you could take a look at that and tell us if you recognise that as a statement that you gave to investigators in this matter previously.

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to tender that 92 bis package at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, if we could put up Exhibit P35, please? Ms. Deda I want to show you a map and whether it comes up on your screen I'll ask you if you can locate your village on the map for us and tell us or show us where it was located vis-a-vis the town of Gjakova or Djakovica. Do you need it blown up a little further or can you read it from there?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you see your village of Guske?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where it's located on the map is where it was in relation to the town of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How big a village was your village? How many houses approximately?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: About 24 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were the -- what was the ethnicity of the people who lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: They were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement, you describe how a few days after the NATO air strikes started in late March 1999, that VJ forces came to your house and gave you and your family one hour to leave. Can you tell us exactly how this happened? Would you tell the Court how you first became aware that something was happening that day?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: On the 29th of March, an army commander came, a Serb army commander came, his name was Dragan, and he told us that we had to abandon the village within an hour and that's what we did. We all left within an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: At the beginning, at the start, we were told to go to Albania but we got to Brekoc. They returned us and then we went to Korenica. We were sent in that direction so we got to Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand from your written statement that you stayed in Korenica I think first for a week in a field and then later on in the house of Prend Markaj for three weeks after that. Then on the 27th of April --

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move, Mr. Hannis, can I ask you, please, to confirm the date on which you say that Dragan came and told you to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would indicate to you, you may see in the last page in the package there was an amendment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A correction, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just ignore that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Deda, if I can take you then to the 27th of April, could you tell the Judges briefly what happened on that day to you and your family at the house of Prend Markaj?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: On the 27th of April, at 6.30 in the morning, the army forces, Serb army forces entered the house in our courtyard and they ordered us to leave the house. We went out, the whole family, and they began to separate the men from the women, the men on one side and the women and the children on the other side. And they started beating the men and robbing them, they were demanding money, valuables. They lined the men up. They forced them to march. We left them where they left us. They forced us to raise three fingers and to shout, "Serbia, Serbia" and their signs, and when we left, 20 metres away, they started shooting. There were bullets flying all over. I returned to find out what was happening to my parents, an uncle, and when I looked back or I looked back, rather, I saw the men lying on the ground. I don't know if they were alive or not, what had happened to them. We continued then on our way to Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Serb forces that you talk about coming to the house that day, can you give us some details about them? Approximately how many were they, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: In the courtyard, when they entered, I think there were about nine, nine people. They had different uniforms. They had army hats, black masks, they didn't have normal army uniforms, did not have normal army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything else about the different uniforms? Colours or markings or insignia?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I didn't really see the insignia. I know that they had scarves, bandanas, and their -- they had hats and so you couldn't see their faces. They had -- the hats were brown, the hoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you were taken outside, where were the men taken?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: We left the men behind in the courtyard, where we were staying with the family. They were lined up and they were being beaten and their money and valuables were taken from them, their rings, what they had in their hands or around their necks. They were lined up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you heard the shots and turned around, how far away from the soldiers away from the men in your family?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't know really. I would think two metres, perhaps three, approximately three. Three metres, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After that date, did you ever see any of those men alive again?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No. My father, we found the body. It was returned from Serbia five years later, in the year 2004, on the 16th of April, we got the body of my father and of my cousin, my other uncles, their bodies came back in 2005 and some of them never returned at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what information did you get at that time about where the bodies had been found?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: They were in mass graves in Serbia. They had been sent there. In the graveyard of Batajnica. My father and uncle and my uncle's son, they were found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Deda, I don't have any further questions of you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we will proceed in this order. Counsel for Ojdanic, Lazarevic, Lukic, Pavkovic, Milutinovic, and Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Deda. I'm Norman Sepenuk and my colleagues here at this table with me, we represent General Ojdanic who is one of the defendants in this case and I'm one of the attorneys representing General Ojdanic. Good afternoon. You testified that on 27th of April, the Serb army forces came to your home; is that correct, Ms. Deda?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes, in the house we were staying at in Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And you stayed -- though you said they were Serb army forces, I believe you also said that they didn't have normal army uniforms; is that correct? I'm sorry, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And some wore hats, correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Some wore masks?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Some wore what, cowboy hats?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And ribbons around their heads, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. The bandanas were all around their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the term "paramilitaries"?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what does that mean to you, the term "paramilitaries"?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't really know how to define it. I heard it during the war that there were paramilitary units who entered certain villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you ever hear -- did you ever see a -- did anybody ever tell you that a certain person was a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And were you ever told that paramilitary sometimes wear things like hats on their heads and ribbons around their necks and masks on their faces? Did you ever hear that?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No one had told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. As I understand it you gave your statement on April 8th, 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how did that come to happen? How did you give a statement? Did certain people come to see you?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And just tell us about that. Where were you at the time and who was it who came to see you?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I was at home. We had returned from the war. And we were interviewed and I told him what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this would have been in April 2000, correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And who was it who came to see you? I see that one of the investigators - I'm not sure I'm pronouncing it correctly - Paulo Pastore Stocchi. Do you remember that person coming to see you?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And was he with anyone?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Just could you -- could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was he there with anyone, for example an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: He was there with an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And prior to that interview on April 8th 2000, can you given a statement or had been requested to give a statement by any other person or group?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what group was that?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: It was the International Crisis Group. That's what they were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you give a statement to that International Crisis Group?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can you recall when that was? We know that the statement you gave to the ICTY, the Tribunal investigators, was April 82000. When would you have given a statement to the International Crisis Group investigator?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't remember the date but it was before the other one, before the statement given to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And could you give us the roughest idea, was it maybe six months before or two months before or can you take -- give us your best estimate on that?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't really remember. I'd remember giving it to them, the statement. I told them about what had happened but I don't remember the date, the exact date, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And was that statement eventually reduced to writing? Did you ever give a written statement to them?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I spoke and they wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I see but they never prepared or did they, did they ever prepare a statement for your later signature? Did you ever read over any statement that they prepared?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So they simply asked you questions and you responded and they wrote down the answers. Is that a fair way to put it?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I told them about all the events, everything that had taken place and they made notes, they took it all down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from them again? Did they ever come back to you to, let's say, verify anything that you had said to them?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you saw them only that one time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, aside from the International Crisis Group, did representatives of any other group -- and I'll be specific here: Did a representative of a group called the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe come to see you?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't remember anyone like that. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Could they have? Can you just search your memory and just once again and see if you can remember, did anybody from that group come to see you at any time?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No. I gave my statement to the International Crisis Group and to the Tribunal. I didn't give any other statement to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So if I were to tell you, and as a matter of fact, would you kindly with would the usher put -- I think Mr. Hannis has something to say here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand why counsel is asking these questions but based on our internal research I think we have an explanation for what is troubling him and it's totally separate from this witness. I don't know if Mr. Sepenuk is willing to take my word on it. It's something that we can explain to him but I don't think he will get much help?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, what we have here Your Honour is a kind -- I very much appreciate the kind offer of hope and I mean that sincerely because I think Mr. Hannis, frankly, is pretty much a straight shooter, I do. I say that sincerely, but we have two statements here, Your Honour, that are word for word. Your Honours have already seen there. We have two statements that are word for word identical from the -- from the OSCE and the International Crisis Group. If the International Crisis Group was the only one who interviewed her then the OSCE is doing what they charged the International Crisis Group with doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the issue here, though, Mr. Sepenuk is what is to be gained by the exercise you're about to embark on. If it's acknowledged that the two statements are identical -- I could see some value in further exploration if there were differences but it seems to me that the explanation for this lies elsewhere, in light of the witness saying what she has said so far. Do you think you require to challenge her further on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh, no. As a matter of fact, I don't intend to challenge her at all. My intention was not to challenge her at all. My intention was just to show that they have two identically worded statements and, if we could, Your Honour before you ultimately decide on - as seen, as told before, unless you've already made the decision - we would like to supplement our arguments with this -- because we think this shows a certain untrustworthiness in the collection process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should supplement that argument by tomorrow. In fact if you do it later today all the better but certainly by tomorrow, end of week. But it seems to me you've made the point you want to make on this. We note the challenge that you're making to the authenticity of these statements and the question mark you raise over them and I don't think any useful purpose would now be served by exploring the issue further with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, and maybe we can do this also by stipulation right now. Will Mr. Hannis stipulate that the descriptions contained in Exhibit -- defendant Exhibit 3D1 and 3D2 are diametrically opposed to much of the information given in the prior statement particularly as it regards VJ soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, Your Honour. I mean, I haven't looked closely at that document. The document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The point is, Your Honour, the statement talks about VJ soldiers. We have a different situation now. When I say the statement, the April 82000 statement, whereas the International Crisis Group statement speaks about police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have no intention of preventing you exploring that, if you feel that's necessary. That's not the issue I'm concerned about. I'm concerned about there question of why there are two documents there that may well be identical, may well be from an identical source or maybe from separate sources. That's something the witness can't help us with. However, it's a different question if you want to explore with her the actual differences in the content of the document. That's separate and that's a matter for you. Equally, of course, we can read them but you've got to make that judgement call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As long as Mr. Hannis started this colloquy -- do you quarrel with what the International Crisis Group wrote in this -- do you claim that it's not what she told them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No I have no -- I have no information to make that claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. So we can accept this 3D1 and 3D2 as what she told the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we can accept that's what she told the investigators from the ICG. Our explanation is that she never spoke to the OSCE and we have some further explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's fine. If you can accept that this is what she told the investigator of the ICG, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can accept that that's what ICG reported she said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two different things there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Then I'll go into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We will put up on the screen, please, 3D2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is one thing I would like to ask the witness before we go into this at all. And it's on a rather separate matter. Ms. Deda, when you spoke of the 24th of March 1999, 24th of March, sorry, the -- sorry, my mistake, the 29th of March, the first matter you were asked questions about when you came in, you referred to a man called Dragan coming to your home. Do you recollect saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you learn the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we knew the name because he was an officer in Korenica so he was known, he had been known earlier as Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. If the usher would put 3D1, actually 3D2. By the way, I would ask Mr. Hannis do you have this in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. It appears that we do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just referring to the incident you described, Ms. Deda, on April 27th, 1999, where certain people came to your home. You've already testified. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: According to this document, which purports to be what you told, a record of what you told to an International Crisis Group investigator, you said that on April 27th, 1999, and I quote now, "Serb police separated and beat the following men." And then there is a number of men listed, Mark Deda and a number of Dedas, Pac Deda, Linton Deda. Can you see it at all on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Actually if you would roll up the screen, please, no, the other way. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see the names listed there? This relates to the incident you described, you say yes?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And is that what you told the investigator from the International Crisis Group, I quote, "Serb police separated and beat the following men"?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. I told them about the case which happened on the 27th, but also later and what happened later when the police separated men from the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And according to this, when you talk about the 27th on the 27th, you supposedly said, or allegedly said to them, at least according to this document, that masked Serb police with painted faces as a paramilitary forces. Paramilitary forced the witness and other villagers and -- out of their houses. Did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Deda, in the statement which you gave to the investigator from this Tribunal, you referred to the things that happened on the 27th of April as being done by VJ soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Various questions have just been asked of you about the conduct of the -- of police officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, please, the question, if you please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question is that -- I'm inviting you to be very careful in your description of the personnel who were involved on the 27th of April and to be sure that you've told us to the best of your recollection the identity of all the people involved on that occasion. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were as I said earlier -- there were some soldiers with hats, some bandanas, and other people with other uniforms. They were wearing different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you mean, then, when a moment ago you said, and let me get the exact words. Yeah, "I told them about the case which happened on the 27th and what happened later when the police separated the men from the women". Who were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not the police but the army, when they entered the courtyard, it was the army, and they separated men from women and children. Women and children, they allowed them to proceed, whereas the men were held there and they were put in a line, they were asking for their money, for their valuables, whatever they had on them, and that's how we left them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to continue along the same lines. Ms. Deda, I'm Djuro Cepic, Defence counsel on the Defence team for General Vladimir Lazarevic. In the proceedings against Slobodan Milosevic, did you testify on the 15th and on the 16th of July 2002?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to confirm for me what you already stated in that trial, that is to say you confirmed that on the critical day, that is to say we are talking about the 27th of April 1999, there was a masked policemen there and there were members of the paramilitary force who is expelled you from your house, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a page citation to the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. [Interpretation] The page is 8081, line 12 through 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Ms. Deda, is what you stated in the proceedings against Slobodan Milosevic correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I wanted to add something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your permission I would like to go back to that question later and now I would like to ask you something else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Did you say, Ms. Deda, you wanted to say something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the question that was asked, I wanted to say that the police, when they forced us out of the home in the courtyard, there were no policemen but there was policemen as well as soldiers on the way as we were leaving but not in the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to what happened in the month of March described on page 2, paragraph 3 of the statement that the witness gave to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 8th of April 2000. The same page and the same paragraph both in the B/C/S version and in the English version. I'm sorry, paragraph 5. I apologise. Ms. Deda, can we consider the village of Bushka [phoen] could be close to the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The villages of Deve and Babaj [phoen], are they also close to the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes, they are closer to the border than our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in that period, the border belt was five kilometres wide?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't know the length of the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know anything about any illegal border crossings? Did you hear people talk about that maybe?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your brother, Pal Deda, did he make any statements to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your mother, did she give any statements to the investigators of the OTP, or any other member of your family?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is stated here is, and now I'm quoting, "On the 25th of March, 1999, in the village of Deve and the village of Babaj, soldiers killed eight men and a day later, commander Dragan came to your village and he took your uncles so that they would bury the bodies of the killed men." Can we infer that the only information that you got about this was obtained from your uncles?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. My uncle told us that Dragan came and asked them to go and bury the corpses and that happened on the 27th of March and not on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know who Dragan is?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I know that he was an army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you make a distinction, though? Do you know whether this Dragan was a commander in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't know. I knew that he was an army commander but no, no further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you, Mrs. Lizane Malaj testified in this courtroom. Do you know her?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I know her by name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. First of all is it Deda or Dedaj? I don't want to mispronounce your name.

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Deda.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Deda, my name is Dan Ivetic, and with my colleague, Mr. Branko Lukic, and today with Mr. Ozren Ogrizovic, I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic, and I thank you for coming here today. I have a few questions to ask for you. First of all, in your statement you stated that the VJ and the police first deployed in the area of your village in autumn of 1998. Would you confirm for us that at that time although traffic stops or check-points were set up, civilians including yourself were able to pass through said check-points without any hindrance?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: There were many check-points everywhere in 1998, and we didn't have any particular problem. Once I was held by the police, and I was told that I had to greet them when I passed by, and otherwise, I haven't had any particular problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And during the same time period, ma'am, would it also be accurate to state that there were not any type of attacks against civilians such as yourself, that is to say in autumn of 1998, all the way through March of 1998? Up to March 29th of 1999.

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. There wasn't any incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would it also be fair to say during that same time period that civilians such as yourself went around their normal daily affairs? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe you indicated that you had gone -- that you went to Djakovica to school every day. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the other parts of civic life, did the hospitals or medical clinics in the area continue to function during that time period?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. They functioned normally but -- they worked normally. Although it was a tense time, they worked normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that is to say Albanian citizens could receive treatment at the hospitals, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the schools that you -- that were attended did you attend a state-run school, that is to say a school set up by the Serbian authorities of Kosovo/Metohija?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: The school I went to, it was the high school. We did not go to the proper schools, the school which was properly for high school students, but we had our lessons in the premises of the elementary schools and that was because the high school premises were controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, did anyone stop -- did any of the Serb authorities stop you from going to school on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't it also true, ma'am, that there were schools set up by the authorities in Kosovo/Metohija that gave courses in both Albanian and the Serbian languages?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I told you earlier that there were schools, there were high schools which were built properly for that purpose but we could not go there for lessons because they were controlled by the Serbs, and we took our lessons in the premises of the elementary schools. So where I took my lessons when I was an elementary school kid, that's where I took the lessons when I was a grown-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that elementary school building, was that also a state-run school? Who set up that school?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who built it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The point is, ma'am, isn't it accurate to say that the Kosovo Albanians, that is to say Kosovo citizens of Albanian ethnicity boycotted Serbian institutions, including the Serbian schools?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: The Albanians did not boycott the schools but they were not allowed to get into the premises of those schools. We did not dare enter those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ever physically prevent you from entering the premises of the high school that you say you could not go to?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Once I was going there and I was stopped at a check-point in Gjakova and the police told me there that whenever you pass by this point, you've got to greet us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a question, Mr. Ivetic, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: At this stage. I'd like to ask you, you said you did not go to the high school because it was closed and under the control of the Serbs, the secondary school that is. And you went to elementary school instead. Now, when you went to elementary school, was your tuition at the elementary level or was it at the secondary level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was at the secondary school level so in the morning, it was the elementary school pupils who took their lessons there and in the afternoon it was the pupils, the students of the high school, who took their lessons in the same building. But the building belonged to the elementary school as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, if I could direct your attention to the transcript, could we get the transcript up in front of the witness or not? Page 78 -- it's in English, that won't help you. I apologise. That won't help her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am isn't it a fact that you testified here earlier today that no one prevented you from going to school?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now the follow-up question I want to ask on that is: Did you ever try or did anyone ever -- any of your classmates ever try to go to the high school, the proper high school building, at which time you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Did not try because there was no teaching taking place there. We went to those premises where the teaching took place. That's where the pupils and the teachers went.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I just ask you one question on that? Do you know who provided the teachers who taught you high school lessons in the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were from Gjakova but as to who paid them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we will adjourn I think at this stage, and we will resume again at 3.30, and I would invite counsel, if possible, to have regard to the sensitivities affecting the witness and if we can complete this evidence today, hopefully we shall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my intention, Your Honour, I only have about 10 to 12 minutes more with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've taken advantage of the pause to go through my questions and the transcript and I've been able to cut down my remaining questions quite a bit to facilitate our goal of finishing this, so I'll only have approximately one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Deda, if I can direct your attention to the last page, that is page 5 in the Albanian, the last paragraph, page 5 in the English, and I believe it's page 4 in the B/C/S, of the statement dated 8 April 2000, and I just have -- I would like to ask if indeed it is correct and true as you stated to the investigators of the Tribunal and I'm going to read there portion here, "The police did not take part to the military operations that I have described in my statement. They were only patrolling the road while we were on the convoy, in the convoy." Is that correct and what you told the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: On the road there were both army and police but in the courtyard where I was, there was no police. There was only the army there. For other places I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Deda. My name is Aleksander Aleksic and I appear here on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. I will have a few questions for you and I will try to be as precise as possible. I would kindly ask you to provide as brief answers as possible, if possible with a simple yes or no. I just wanted to draw the attention of the Chamber that because of the intended line of questioning, I will probably have to repeat a couple of questions previously used by my learned friends. But I will try to stay as brief as possible. Mrs. Deda, you gave a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal and if I understood correctly, you have a hard copy in Albanian in front of you. The paragraph I want to refer to is on page 2 as regards e-court in the English that is page 10. In the Albanian, this is the fourth paragraph where you say, "I went on foot daily to my school in Djakovica and I never had any problems when I had to pass through police check-points." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have any problems, just one time, I was told that we were supposed to greet the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph, just below that, you state, "On the 24th of March, 1999, the NATO air strikes against Serbia started. From that day on, my family and myself could not go out any more." Is that correct? Is this what you stated?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Since it is not in dispute that you testified in the Milosevic case, I wanted to remind you of a portion of your testimony there, on page 8074, dated the 15th of July 2002, line 12, line 13. In your answer to Mr. Milosevic's question you stated that you could not go outside and leave because there was a police check-point nearby. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To move on to another topic, after these events, once you left your house and when you were part of the convoy, during the journey there were no particular problems, there were no murders, rapes or anything of that nature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: When we left Guske, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, if you would turn the page, please, in the Albanian, as regards the English, it is on the same page, page 10. In e-court, the last paragraph. As for the Albanian, it is on the next page, the second paragraph. You state there, "On the way to Korenica, VJ vehicles escorted us." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: To continue, in the same paragraph, you say that "during that week, I did not see any crime committed there." Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: During NATO bombings, in that area, there were quite a few local criminals there who posed great problems, they created problems?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, counsel, Mr. Aleksic, but there is no page 10 in the English translation, both for this last passage which you're referring to and the one previously. The one previously was at page 2 but I don't know if you could get an indication as to the page and the correct page in English for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that it was page 10 in the -- in e-court, in the English version, but whereas -- as for the hard copy, this is indeed page 2. In e-court, we have a single document for both the English and the Serbian versions. I will now go back to the transcript from the Milosevic case, page 8093 dated the 16th of July 2002, line 20 and line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: There you state, "The valley --" if I may have a moment to locate that precisely. "The valley was full, the roads were full of criminals and people wearing scarves and so on and so forth." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. When we left Korenica, that was what it was like. The army was there, they were masked, they were wearing black masks, hats. When we left Korenica that's what it was like on the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In that same transcript from the Milosevic case -- I apologise, this is page 8082, lines 5 to 11. You were asked a question and you provided an answer as to what had happened in your village. You told Mr. Milosevic, "You know well what happened there. You know that better than I do." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: You mean that's what I said to Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in your next answer, you said, "You know what happened there because you issued that order." Is that correct? Did you say that to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any such order pertaining to the village of Guske issued by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any written letter or any written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you hear Mr. Milosevic ordering anything regarding the village of Guske?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear anything like that but he was the head of Serbia and he was head of the army; he was the one who decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions, Your Honour, and I have an arrangement I made with Mr. Hannis. As for the witness, she may be permitted to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would say regarding the arrangement we have there are I think two places in her statement where Mr. Fila felt it was somewhat confusing. I think it's clear, and based on my conversations with letter and her prior answers, I'm satisfied as to what it means. We agree about that but I don't know if the Court is willing to accept what we agree about what she says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not sure I understand that because you have to bear in mind that there are the interests of six accused involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No matter what understanding you may have with Mr. Fila, anything goes when it comes to submissions toe end of the day if the matter is open to interpretation so if you feel you have to explore anything further then it's a matter for you to judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't but Mr. Fila didn't want to burden the witness with anything if he didn't have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's his judgement. Mr. Fila, if you want to review your position, it's a matter for you. Are you content to leave the matter or do you want to explore anything with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't want to examine this witness. I just wanted to point out to a fact that there might be a misunderstanding in the transcript. If I had any questions for the witness, I wouldn't doubt her answers. I tried to check the transcript on the other hand rather than to cross-examine and perhaps it's best for Mr. Hannis to read out the transcript himself. There is a word missing. It seems that a witness had uttered a word which hasn't been entered into the transcript. I just didn't want to burden the witness unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I can deal with what we've talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Deda, in your statement in paragraph 7, I think it's numbered on your copy, you talked about the events on the 29th of March when you were ordered to leave your house and the convoy went to Korenica or moved from Korenica and arrived at Meja where in your statement you say, "the VJ stopped the convoy and ordered the people to go and stay in different houses in Korenica." So had you actually gotten as far as Meja and then you were told to go back to Korenica and stay there?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the other question I have for you relates to paragraph -- let's see, paragraph 9, that's two paragraphs down from that. On the 27th of April, you say, "the VJ soldiers came to our house and forced us to leave." On the 27th of April, you weren't staying in Guske at your family home, correct? You were in Korenica at somebody else's house? And that was the house of Prend Markaj?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I just have a couple of other questions. You answered Mr. Ivetic when he was asking you about going to school, and you said that's "we did not dare enter on those premises of the high school, the Serb-controlled high school." Why did you not dare to enter those premises?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: It was closed. There was no teaching going on there. The secondary school was closed. There were only Serbs who could go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And why was there no teaching being provided at the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I only know that only Serbs went in there and the teachers our teachers didn't dare go into the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean the Albanian teachers?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic also asked you about the last paragraph in your statement where you said that the police were only patrolling the road when you were in the convoy. The police patrolling the road, can you tell us what kind of uniforms they wore? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Had they wore camouflaged uniforms in two colours. I don't know how to explain it any better. Police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what colour?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: They were -- they wore a light and dark-blue colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know of any police to wear different coloured uniforms or are those the only uniforms that you associate with the police?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: There are other police uniforms, which are lighter, a light colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last one I had, I think it was Mr. Aleksic directed you to a portion of the transcript from your testimony on 15 July in 2002 in the Milosevic case where he read a part of your answer on page 8074 at line 12. The question that you were asked by Mr. Milosevic was, "From the 24th of March when the NATO air strikes began against Serbia, why could you and your family not go out any more?" Mr. Aleksic read the first sentence of your answer which was, "we didn't dare to go out because the police had a check-point there." The rest of your answer was, "They were everywhere and they would take all the men away." Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that what the situation was at that time after the NATO air strikes?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: Yes. The police and the army were everywhere. There were even more after the beginning of the bombing campaign and the police, the army was on constant movement around. We didn't dare to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Judge Chowhan has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it will be a very small short question. You spoke of people wearing masks when you saw them in that position of firing and riding. Now if they were wearing masks, how were you able to identify them? And could you please also tell us what type of masks they were wearing and what other methods they were adopting to camouflage themselves and how could you get to know the identity? I'm very grateful. I'm sorry to bother you.

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: When they originally came into the courtyard of Prend Markaj, they were wearing black masks. You could only see their eyes and they wore black masks but there were also some with hats and some with bandanas around their heads. I saw them. They came into the courtyard like that. And they separated the men from the women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But how did you find out who they were accurately?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: I don't know who they were. I imagine they were the army. They took the men away and killed them but I don't know their names, who they were personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Deda, thank you very much -- sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of Judge Chowhan's question I'd like to ask one question if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Deda, what language were these soldiers speaking who came to your house on the 27th of April?

utterances.speaker: Merita Deda
utterances.text: They spoke Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is there any matter arising from these various questions of Judge Chowhan and Mr. Hannis that any Defence counsel wishes to raise? All right. Thank you very much. Well, that completes your evidence, Ms. Deda. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Before the next witness comes in, I can raise a procedural matter which we feel may affect the witness who is scheduled to testify as early as tomorrow. I'd like to address you on that at some point before we end the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It relates to the witness Nike Peraj who may in fact begin his testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're raising my hopes when you tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, there are two matters in relation to him.
