He's now been designated as an 89(F) witness and under your order on the 11th of July, the order on procedure and evidence the Prosecution is obligated to provide his 89(F) statement at least 48 hours in advance of his testimony in both English and the language of the accused. We received neither to this point. Neither the English or the B/C/S. And the second point is this morning we received a document, some disclosure in relation to this witness which is in English only. Again not translated into the language of the accused. So we are very concerned that our clients --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was that item? The disclosure that you say was in English only?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's a four page document, notes on statements made by Nike Peraj during telephone conversation of 11 July 2005, a telephone conversation with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And would English appear to be the language in which the notes were made originally?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It would appear so because I don't believe there is a B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is there an obligation to translate something of that nature disclosed to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, for consultation with our clients. It's a statement of the -- Mr. Peraj under 66(A)(ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter of interpretation perhaps but if it was simply a document that was being disclosed to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We say it's tantamount to proofing notes and proofing notes by definition are statements of the accused -- of a witness. It should come to us and be translated into the language of the accused for the accused to be able to consult with his counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stamp, could you deal with this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour. There are a couple of issues here, first those notes are notes of an interview on a telephone that was conducted sometime ago with the witness. They are not -- they do not comprise a statement or any statement of the witness under Rule 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean they are not what the witness said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They are what the witness stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a statement, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, there have been a lot of judicial interpretation of what Rule 66 refers to. Rule 66 refers to a statement a formal statement given to the OTP, and those notes are in a conversation which our investigator might have with a witness and you would imagine there were dozens of conversations that investigators might have with witnesses over four or five years. Any conversation are the record or notes of any conversation would not necessarily fall under Rule 66. However the practice has been that if they involve anything significant, then we would disclose those notes as a matter of fairness to the Defence. But they are not a part of the witness's statement and therefore, they do not there is no requirement that they be translated under Rule 66. The second aspect of the submission is in respect to the material the Rule 89(F) material for the witness. The Court did order that the 89(F) material should be disclosed 48 hours before. Now there seems to be a little bit of a misunderstanding. The witness testified in the Milosevic case under Rule 92 bis so there is a Rule 92 bis package for the witness. About Monday or Friday, I can't recall exactly but I could provide the exact date and time, the 89(F) notification with the translations into B/C/S was admitted to the Defence. Sorry? And that was a 92 bis documentation from the Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's it that will be what's presented?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I go on because it becomes slightly more complicated. That package and I call it a package because it is composed of three statements, one of them very lengthy and one of them of moderate length, and when he came here this week, and has been proofed, he had other information which I thought should go into his statement so I found myself in a position with four statements. I thought instead of doing the proofing notes which my friend spoke of and having regard to the difficulty I saw the Court having this week with four or five different statements, especially that deal with the same narrative incident, you know, moving from one statement to another to find what is said, that I could put all of them into one statement which is what I'm trying to do. The other problem is two of those previous statements are not paragraphed, so I thought it would be convenient to the Court to provide a formal 89(F) statement which is just a composite of all three previous statements plus the proofing notes where everything will be organised with paragraph numbers. So in the course of what I suspect the Defence will agree with me would be a witness of some interest and they might be some cross-examination, it could run smoothly and efficiently. So this latter 89(F) statement is an attempt on my part to assist the Court and to help the proceedings to move more efficiently when the witness comes. It is a composite of the previous statements which were disclosed to the Defence on Monday according or in accordance with your order that it be disclosed 48 hours before, plus the proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have they -- have the proofing notes been disclosed at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The proofing notes are part of that document and the proofing notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are talking about the additional information you obtained at the beginning of the week in the proofing. Has that been disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The additional information is a part of that document which the Defence has, which is in English. What I'm trying to do to make -- as I said what I'm trying to do is to put everything into one document where the additional information composed of about three or four new paragraphs is clearly marked and that we are trying to get a rush translation done for that and we are trying to have the English disclosed to the Defence as soon as possible. I think at the next break. The B/C/S draft disclosed to the Defence sometime this afternoon. It will be a draft and we will trying to get an official B/C/S translation to put on the EDS for tomorrow. Not the EDS, the e-court for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, being realistic in this are we going to reach him tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To some degree it depends on how the next witness goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it not possible simply to put him back and replace -- well, to put him back and bring someone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It will not be possible to bring anyone. There are two witnesses before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps they will take the rest of today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But let's assume that they do that, and then on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you not bring someone else on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think notice -- I'm not completely familiar with the arrangements for bringing witnesses but I could say off-hand that the notice would be too short to bring somebody from Albania for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's -- I've said it before, I'll say it again it seems to me a crazy system, this proofing days before a witness is supposed to give evidence when there has been a lengthy pre-trial phase in the case. I cannot, still cannot understand why the Prosecution don't have lawyers go over statements with witnesses much earlier so that the final statements are available well before the witness is due to testify. I can see that this will be an ongoing problem in the trial as long as that practice persists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I entirely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I commend the efforts you're making to combine it all into one and that it would plainly be of assistance to have that and not -- so far as it can be avoided and not moving between a number of documents. And if I have understood entirely what you've said, then the Defence already have all but a few paragraphs already translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All of this, all of it but four paragraphs, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you very much. Only two things. [Interpretation] First of all, as regards the discussion about whether this is a statement or not, I can only tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything you say on that matter can only weaken your position. I would counsel you to say no more. What's the second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second point is this: This witness is not just an ordinary witness. He has provided a long and elaborate statement. Actually there are a few statements that he provided. And what Mr. Stamp is saying now about a few paragraphs may appear as a lengthy addition which is very simple and very straightforward, but as far as we are concerned, as far as our investigation is concerned, this may be very -- a very lengthy process. We had a conversation before the disclosure of his statement according to Rule 89(F) and we heard that this witness would speak about the crime bases or who was an immediate participant, and if we did not have a number of pieces of evidence to show we would have accepted a shorter term, but when it comes to this witness and when it comes to the cross-examination, you will see that we want to do a very long cross-examination. Any new piece of information requires a certain reorganisation of the job that I'm not sure that we will be able to do within the next 12 hours, if we don't get to bed at all tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, but we have already decided there is no answer to the two points made by Mr. O'Sullivan. In our opinion, in this context, the record of conversation which is supposed to be a verbatim record of what the witness said falls within 66(A)(ii) and if the practice has been that that should be disclosed and translated form then that must be translated. The rule doesn't require that but that seems to be the practice that's followed. And secondly, the four paragraphs are undoubtedly also within Rule 66(A)(ii) and therefore they have to be disclosed timeously, in the language of the accused in accordance with the practice. So there will allowed to the Defence the necessary time. However, that may be weekend time. There is always a sting in the tail. I think what's clear from this is that the witness can't start giving evidence tomorrow, but as long as these matters are dealt with between now and tomorrow, then he can start on Monday. Obviously, in every case, that's subject to something unexpected emerging or unforeseen emerging, whereupon appropriate applications would be made by anyone affected. Just in case there are difficulties, I would hope that for Monday the Prosecution have in hand other possible witnesses. So that's how the matter will be dealt with on the information presently available. We can now, I think, proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It I just briefly? We accept the ruling and the Prosecution is guided by it and ensure that the order is complied with, but, however, it may well be that in the course of the case we'll need clarification on that. What are called proofing notes, as Your Honour can well imagine, almost any time a witness has spoken to by a different person there might be something that is apparently new and significant, and it is the practice of the Prosecution that we disclose it to the Defence. If additional information, when the witnesses come to The Hague -- or should I put it this way, if additional information elicited from the witness when they come to The Hague and disclose to the Defence may leave the Prosecution in a position where the testimony of the witness is postponed, then it is possible that of the over 100 witnesses that we have we are going to find ourselves in this situation quite frequently. And I agree that the ideal situation is that we should probably go and talk to all the witnesses in all the cases sometime before but we -- there is not sufficient resources to bring them here before they testify for proofing, send them back, and then bring them back immediately before they testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I understand the Prosecution's attitude to this, and the reasons that the Prosecutor herself thinks justify this course of action. But bear in mind that some of the accused here spent over two years in custody while allegedly an investigations were being carried out into the case, and some, I think, were here from the year -- were before the Court from the year 2002 and one would expect that, with such a lengthy pre-trial process, things would be in order when the trial got going. So I have to say that I am not terribly sympathetic to the overall proposition or the proposition that this will affect a large number of witnesses. I am, however, likely to be sympathetic to an unforeseen development that occurs, that affects the Prosecution. But it seems to me that if you envisage a general problem, then you're going to be required to take steps to avoid that problem occurring. One of the remedies open to the -- in fact, there are wide-ranging remedies open to the Court where there is a failure to comply with the disclosure obligations. The Pre-Trial Judge or the Trial Chamber may decide proprio motu or if he request of either party for sanctions to be imposed on a party which fails to perform its disclosure obligations pursuant to the rules. Now, it may be that delaying the proofing exercise results in a failure to disclose, a failure to perform disclosure obligations. So you should be alert to that but for the moment, we confine what we say in the form of an order to the circumstances affecting this very important witness. And we leave it to you to try to make arrangements to ensure that the paperwork is in a fit state for his evidence to begin on Monday. Meanwhile, we'll proceed to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, as it pleases you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is Martin Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading what is placed in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. We are all aware, Mr. Pnishi, that you have provided information which has been recorded in writing and is before us. But in the case of all witnesses who have done so in this case, there will also be further examination by questions in court, and that's why you're here today. You're in the same position as every other witness giving evidence in this case. These questions will be asked by a number of people representing the Prosecution and the various accused here. They are acting in a professional capacity and as part of their job in some instances may have to challenge your answers or ask you questions which appear to be difficult to answer. That is just part of the process that is followed in this Tribunal. If we consider that anyone asks something inappropriate then we will interrupt the process but in the absence of any sign of interruption from the Judges, then the task for you is quite simply to answer each of the questions posed to the best of your ability. The first person to ask you questions will be the representative of the Prosecutor, and that will be Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you please state your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Martin Kole Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in 1999, were you living in Meja village in the municipality of Gjakova?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you're a farmer?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prior to that, up until 1983, you were a police officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pnishi, as His Honour indicated, we have already the statement that you referred to so I'm going to take you quickly through one or two aspects of it. But before I do, Your Honour, may I just indicate that the two statements referred to are P2236. I don't think I need take him through identifying his signature unless there are objections. They were part of the 92 bis package presented before. Can you recall the 22nd of April 1999? Did anything significant happen in the district where you live?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In one or two sentences, can you tell me what happened -- tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: The 22nd of April, at about 17 hours, it was in the village of Meja, in the village of Meja, a criminal militant, Prascevic, with another four associates of his, were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean by criminal militant Prascevic? What was the office or position of this person and his associates?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: I can say that he did all that he could do and I'm talking about what he did in the Gjakova municipality. He did whatever he wanted to do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pnishi, remember we don't have a lot of time and so I'm going to ask you just to focus on answering my questions with precision. Can you tell us what was the official job title of Prascevic and the four persons or four associates that were killed on the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: He was the head of the police department in the Gjakova municipality, and he has done, he did whatever he wanted to do and whatever he could do, and he has killed a lot of people, he had -- he has beaten up, he beat up a lot of people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, after Mr. Pascevic was killed, did anything happen in your community? Now I'm going to ask you to tell me if anything happened in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: After he was killed, the convoys of police and military forces came from Gjakova to the village of Meja and they were shooting at houses, they came to the scene of the -- of what happened. They were shooting from the road to all houses along the road, so they fired automatic rifles, they fired at my brother's house and they had to lie flat on the ground to avoid being shot and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the 23rd of April, did you leave with your family to go and stay with persons in the village of Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: That's true. That night, all the neighbours came to my cellars and they took shelter there, and we were altogether 60 people, women, elderly and the following day we went to a nearby village to get some more shelter there near the mountains and for a few days there was no offensive up until the 27th when the main offensive started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the morning of the 27th you returned from Jahoc to your home in Meja, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We came to feed the animals. I returned with my wife and soon after, my son came, to feed the cows, the pigs and the hens but then we had to go to Jahoc, but thousands of police, military, and other forces cropped up unexpectedly in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very quickly, in your statement, remember that we have your statement so again I'm going to ask you to be as precise as possible. In your statement you said that four men, including police and soldiers, brought somebody by the name of Kole Dushmani to your house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They found Kole Dushmani and he slept at his daughter's house and then he was coming back by bicycle to his village in Korenica and then they stopped him and in front of my house, they beat him, then they asked him, "Whose house is this?" And then he told them it was Martin Pnishi's house they broke into my place and they -- they told us to go to Albania to leave, they were -- behaved brutally with me. They fired -- they fired their automatic weapons on the ground or in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you said that they wore masks. Did all of them wear masks or did only some of them wear masks?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Two policemen, they were wearing their uniforms and they were wearing masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: But the two Russians didn't have masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I was about to ask you about the two Russians anyway. The two Russians, how did you know that they were Russians? What language did they speak?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: They were speaking Russian, strasvoji [phoen], and so on. I used to learn Russian at school. I picked up a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you also said that they were in your statement, they wore green camouflage uniforms; is that correct? Was it green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the Russians?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: It was the Serbian police with camouflage, whereas the Russians were wearing blue colour uniforms and grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- you said that they took Kole to your brother's house. Did you see them take him --

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- to your brother's house and if so, where were you when they took him into your brother's house?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: I saw with my own eyes because they brought him first to my door and when they asked me to lie on the ground, Kole said, "Well, be courageous" and then someone started speaking Russian. They -- then they left me lying on the ground and they took Kole to my brother's house. I went out to the -- to watch from the window and I could see him being taken into the courtyards of my brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Bench ask the witness to speak much more slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, could you try to remember to answer my questions as precisely as possible and speak slowly so that the translators can get down every word you say? So we can get a good record much what you're saying. What I want to know is -- well, you said in your statement that you heard many shots coming from your brother's house after they took Kole into your brother's house. What I really want to know, how long after you saw them taking him into your brother's house did you hear these shots coming from your brother's house?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: I heard the shots as soon as they entered the house of my brother. Soon after that I heard shots being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you estimate the time, when you say "soon"? Could you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Not even a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us what became of Kole? Did you ever see him alive again?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: I have not -- I didn't see him alive after that. 19 days after what happened, we went to check in my brother's house what had happened. When we entered the house we found Kole lying down, and we managed to identify him and that he was Kole Dushmani.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you notice about him when you went to your brother's house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, this is quite detailed examination, Mr. Stamp, of matters which are clearly recorded in the statement. If it's to be supplemented, fine, or if there is something you wish to emphasise but we don't want to go through the whole statement when we've got it here to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the condition of your brother's house when you went back to it 19 days later?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: The house of my brother is just over five -- ten metres further away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So what happened to your brother's house when you went back there and saw it?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: The house was burned, and Kole Dushmani's body was lying on the ground. He was dead. And when we searched further, we could see like 15 bullet holes on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You've indicated in your statement that you saw the police pushing or escorting seven young men along the Ura e Traves bridge and then they shot those men. And you later said that one of the policemen included Predrag Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you go on to that, sorry, I'm going back to the points where I interrupted you. Now that you've taken some more material, can I just clarify one thing with the witness in relation to the question which I did interrupt? Mr. Pnishi, you were asked by Mr. Stamp what did you notice about the -- Kole Dushmani's body when you went to your brother's house. Could you answer that now, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. His body was lying on the kitchen floor, and all that was in the kitchen was burned down, and we could see, we could see, we could see that -- a drawing around his body on the same day we got his body and organised the quick burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you tell from his body how he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bullets, bullet holes that could be seen, it was just in the front part of his body, and they had -- they had penetrated his body and fallen on to the wall, you could see the holes there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there many bullet holes on his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many, there were. On the wall we could see 15 to 16 holes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, one question. Excuse me, please. What was the condition of the body? Because you went and saw it after a few days. Did the body suffer from putrefaction or was it all looking -- a fresh, dead body lying there? That condition I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I may explain that. The body was lying on the floor, on the cement. It was not burned. There was -- there was smoke inside the walls which remained there, and it -- the -- it was not burned, and it was not -- it was preserved in this way so it was not decomposed because of the smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say later that day you sought refuge in your Godfather's house in Jahoc and from your Godfather's house you saw seven young men who were shot on the bridge, Ura e Traves. When you saw these men being shot, how far were you away from them?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Close enough that I left my place I went to my Godfather's house and from the third floor, in aerial -- in aerial distance it was like 50 metres away where these seven young men were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said that you could identify one of the policemen who shot these seven men. Can you say his name, please?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Predrag Stanojevic -- Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him before, from the 1970s onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you knew him to be a police officer? And if so, from -- attached to which department?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes. He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he was attached to which police department?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: In Gjakova police force he worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also in your statement said Dragutin, the police commander in Panoshec was among those who were separating the men from women and children in Meja Rize [phoen]. Who is this Dragutin? Have you ever discovered -- well, who was he?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Dragutin was Stojanovic, nicknamed Guta. He was a police commander in Panoshec. He took his car in Korenica and he blocked the road with his car so when all the tractors and cars came there they had to stop. So he set up kind of a check-point there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you Mr. Pnishi. Is Dragutin Stojanovic nicknamed Guta the same Stojanovic who you saw shooting the seven young men?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Stanojevic, Stojanovic, it's one letter which makes the difference between the two names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So there are two persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, they are two different persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we quickly show the witness I know I'm going over the planned time but could we quickly show the witness map P35? And could you pan so that we could have a close-up view of the surrounding area, the area surrounding Djakovica? Can you see that map, sir? Can you make out the town of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are just about four or five things I'd like you to point out on the map but I'd also like to you mark it so perhaps the usher could assist. Now, excuse me, is that something that will mark it? Okay. Well, he should -- Mr. Pnishi, if you touch the thing with that, it will mark it. So what I'd like you to do is mark with an H where your house is located at. Can you point to where your house is located at first?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes. The house is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your house. Can you mark where your house is located on that map with an H? You may need to come closer to it or it may need to be brought closer to you.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: With an H?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So that for the record because this doesn't look like -- very much like an H, the witness has marked on the road just below where it is written Orize, with a red H. Now, you said you escaped to your brother's house which was close to the mountains in the village of Jahoc so that would be I take it further away from --

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: The house of my godfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, your godfather. Can you identify it first on the map and mark it with a G?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Right here is the house of my godfather. Do I need to place a G here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please. Make sure you know where it is first before you write it. Okay. That --

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: It's at the entrance of the village at the bridge. This is -- this is my house and a further 50 metres away is my godfather's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record he puts another mark, a G, just beside the J in Jahoc. I'd like you to put a cross where the bridge was, where these seven men were shot, a small cross.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: This is where the bridge is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness has placed a mark below the -- beside the word Orize in brackets, and the mark also touches on the O in Orize spelled O-r-i-z-e now you said that while you were at your house, that is your house which adjoins the road, you saw a huge crowd coming from Guske and Korenica villages?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you mark along the road where you saw this huge crowd travelling? Identify it first and then mark it.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Guske is here, Korenica is here, and the people of the Guske village were all gathered together and they were being escorted by police towards Korenica and the road is here. And when they came in this direction where I put my hand, and here, they were stopped by the police commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This exercise doesn't help us because we don't see what he's indicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm trying to take it step by step but the witness needs to identify exactly where it is before he marks. So it's his mental process, I think, of identifying where it is. I'm about to invite him to mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mark, please, for me where it is, this large crowd moving from a -- Guske and Korenica villages were travelling and put an arrow in the direction that they were going to, if you could just draw a line along the road.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: They come along this road. They came along this road, up to here, and here they were stopped, all of them were stopped here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put a circle at the point where they were stopped?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: A circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is where Guta placed his car, across the road?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly in that crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said also you saw people coming from Junik towards Meja. Could you put a large circle around Junik? Can you see Junik on that map?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes. That's where Junik is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Please put a circle around the Junik and draw a line with an arrow along the road that they were travelling on, please. An arrow pointing in the direction that they were going.

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you saw the people along that road, where did you see them? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: All these villages, more than 20 villages, the population of these villages were all gathered along this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you mark it?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Up to the entrance to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you mark a line all along the road passing all of those villages where you say the population were forced to walk? Could you mark the entire route that you're speaking of on the map?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: The population of all these villages were gathered and walked along this road which I've marked and they stopped here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, where is this on the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the English copy at page 4. It's in the first paragraph, that paragraph begins on the preceding page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see we've gone back. Sorry, yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you're saying that the population of all the villages along where you just marked were expelled and were moving past your home?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The area that we are talking about, is that the area normally referred to as the Carragojs valley?

utterances.speaker: Martin Pnishi
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we call it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, Your Honour is indictment 72 subparagraph H 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That will be the examination-in-chief, may it please, Your Honour. I'm sorry, most importantly could we save a snapshot of that before it's moved and could it be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sabbah I think you should say what the number is in this instance. It's P35 and we add what? IC?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour, that will be Exhibit IC3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sabbah, what time remains?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because of the way in which the afternoon has been divided up there is not going to be time to engage in cross-examination this afternoon. And it's a suitable place to adjourn. Mr. O'Sullivan, you could perhaps indicate to me the order in which you anticipate the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The order will be counsel for Ojdanic, Lukic, Pavkovic, Lazarevic, Milutinovic, and Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pnishi, that brings the proceedings here to an end for today. You will have to return, though, tomorrow morning to continue with your evidence -- could we have some quiet in the courtroom, please? You will require to return to continue your evidence and that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. You should be here in good time ready to resume your evidence at 9.00. Meanwhile, over night, it's very important that you have no discussion with anyone at all about your evidence. That's either the evidence you have already given or the evidence that you may yet give tomorrow. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court is now adjourned until 9.00 a.m. tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 11th day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
